implementation_notes: Stage one is a plain POCO viewmodel assembled by the controller action; Microsoft's own guidance calls the strongly typed model the most robust way to pass data to a view, and because the type is part of the view declaration the compiler checks the page's shape. Stage two is the channel's renderer: a Razor .cshtml view for HTML, JsonResult or ContentResult for JSON and text, a view component when a region needs its own renderer. Keep channel hints out of the viewmodel (no HTML classes, no JSON field names) so a new channel is a new renderer; only then can view discovery, layout and partial views be changed without touching the page builder. This is the default .NET route - prefer the sibling XSLT variant when the same logical page must also be published as a styled XML artefact.
code_sketch:
public record InvoiceVm(string Customer, string Total);       // stage 1: logical page

[HttpGet("/invoice/{id}")]
public IActionResult Invoice(int id) => View(BuildVm(id));    // HTML channel: Views/Invoice.cshtml

[HttpGet("/invoice/{id}.json")]
public IActionResult InvoiceJson(int id) => Json(BuildVm(id));// JSON channel, same page
pitfalls: ViewData/ViewBag bypass the typed logical page and are resolved at runtime, so controller code starts carrying presentation again - prefer the viewmodel.
A viewmodel that mirrors the ORM entity drags lazy navigation properties into the renderer, executing queries while the view renders and coupling presentation to persistence.

Razor views are compiled with the app, so a broken renderer normally surfaces at build time - but runtime view locations (absolute paths, custom IViewLocationExpander) move that failure back to request time.

variants.name: XDocument logical page + XslCompiledTransform stylesheet
variants.implementation_notes: Build the logical page as an XDocument or XmlDocument and render it with XslCompiledTransform: Load compiles the stylesheet once, Transform executes it per request into a stream, StringWriter or file. This is the pattern's literal .NET form and the right choice when the same page must also be published as XML; the class implements XSLT 1.0 only, and Microsoft disables XSLT scripting and the document() function by default for security, so enable them only for stylesheets you control.
pitfalls: XSLT 1.0 only: XSLT 2.0/3.0 constructs silently do not work, so modern stylesheets need a third-party processor.
The class is annotated RequiresDynamicCode and generates IL at run time, which matters for AOT or trimmed deployments.
Stylesheets are trusted input by design: enabling scripting or document() for an untrusted stylesheet is remote code and file access.
